exposure: Mode of birth (vaginal vs. caesarean section)
outcome: Neonatal gastrointestinal colonization (measured by amplicon sequence variants - ASVs)
cohort: The study included 63 neonates (23 vaginally-born and 40 caesarean section-born) and their mothers, from whom maternal vaginal and rectal swabs were collected before delivery, and neonatal fecal samples were collected at day 0, 7, and 28 postnatally.
finding: Only a limited amount of ASVs were transferred from maternal rectal and vaginal compartments to the neonatal gastrointestinal tract, with ASVs from the maternal gastrointestinal tract contributing to neonatal gut colonization to a greater extent than ASVs from the maternal genital tract at one month of age.
mod_finding: There were no differences in the relative abundance of shared ASVs with maternal vaginal swabs between vaginally- and caesarean section-born neonates, and only a difference on day 7 in shared rectal swabs, with higher relative abundance of ASV shared with the maternal rectal swab in both delivery routes compared to the vaginal swab on day 28.
